final_note: You worked through C3.2 Defence against disease — 18 guide statements.

concepts.def: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted to a host. It is distinguished from non-infectious diseases such as genetic disorders or deficiency diseases, which are not caused by another organism and cannot be transmitted from one person to another by infection.

concepts.term: Careful observation as a source of progress (NOS)
concepts.def: Careful observation of patterns can lead to important progress even before the underlying mechanism is known. In 19th-century Vienna, Semmelweis observed that deaths from childbed fever were far higher on the ward staffed by doctors who came from dissecting corpses than on the ward staffed by midwives, and showed that hand-washing in chlorinated lime reduced deaths. In London in 1854, Snow mapped cholera deaths, found they clustered around the Broad Street water pump and had its handle removed. Both acted decades before the germ theory of disease was accepted and the bacteria responsible were generally recognized.

The barriers that prevent pathogens from entering the body in the first place, as opposed to the immune responses that act once a pathogen is inside. The skin and the mucous membranes are the primary defences.

concepts.term: Skin as a physical and chemical barrier
concepts.def: The skin is a physical barrier because its outer layer consists of tough dead cells that pathogens cannot easily penetrate. It is also a chemical barrier: sebum secreted by sebaceous glands contains fatty acids that keep the surface at a low pH, which inhibits the growth of many pathogens.

The moist lining of surfaces that open to the outside, including the airways, the digestive tract, the reproductive tract and the eyes. These surfaces lack the tough dead outer layer of skin, but the mucus they secrete traps pathogens so that they can be removed, for example by cilia or by swallowing, before they can penetrate the epithelium.

A small cell fragment in the blood, without a nucleus, formed from large cells in the bone marrow. When a blood vessel is damaged, platelets adhere to the damaged site and release clotting factors that start the clotting cascade.

Substances released by platelets (and from damaged tissue) at the site of a cut that initiate the clotting cascade. Without their release, the cascade does not start, so clots do not form in undamaged vessels.

A sequence of reactions, started by the release of clotting factors, in which each step activates the next. Because each activated enzyme molecule can act on many molecules of the next component, the cascade amplifies the initial signal, which is why the final conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by thrombin is rapid.
The enzyme produced at the end of the clotting cascade. Thrombin catalyses the rapid conversion of the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin at the site of damage.

Fibrinogen is a soluble protein that circulates in the plasma of healthy people all the time. Thrombin converts it into fibrin, an insoluble protein that forms a mesh of fibres across the wound. The mesh traps erythrocytes (and platelets) to form a clot that seals the cut.

The part of the immune system that responds to broad categories of pathogen rather than to particular ones, and that does not change during an organism's life: it responds in the same way to a pathogen however many times that pathogen is encountered. Phagocytes are the component of the innate system that IB students need to know.

The part of the immune system, based on lymphocytes, that responds in a specific way to particular pathogens and builds up a memory of the pathogens encountered, so that the response to a pathogen becomes faster and more effective on later exposures.

A white blood cell of the innate immune system that recognizes pathogens as foreign, engulfs them by endocytosis and digests them using enzymes from lysosomes. Phagocytes are not specific to a particular pathogen: the same cell can engulf many kinds.

Movement of a cell by extending its cytoplasm and flowing into the extension, as an amoeba does. Phagocytes use it to squeeze out between the cells of a capillary wall and crawl through tissues to sites of infection.

The process by which a phagocyte engulfs a pathogen: the plasma membrane extends around the pathogen and fuses to enclose it in a vesicle inside the cell. The pathogen does not pass through the membrane into the cytoplasm; it remains inside the vesicle, where lysosomes fuse with it and their enzymes digest it.

A membrane-bound vesicle in the cytoplasm containing hydrolytic enzymes. In a phagocyte, lysosomes fuse with the vesicle containing an engulfed pathogen and their enzymes digest it, keeping the enzymes separated from the phagocyte's own cytoplasm.
A white blood cell of the adaptive immune system. Lymphocytes both circulate in the blood and are contained in lymph nodes. B-lymphocytes and helper T-lymphocytes cooperate to produce antibodies.

A lymphocyte that can produce antibodies. An individual has a very large number of different B-lymphocytes, and each one makes a single specific type of antibody, determined before the cell ever meets an antigen. Only the B-lymphocytes whose antibody fits a particular antigen respond to it.

A small organ on a lymph vessel in which large numbers of lymphocytes are contained. Lymph draining from the tissues passes through lymph nodes, bringing antigens into contact with the lymphocytes there; the nodes swell during infection as lymphocytes multiply.

A protein produced by B-lymphocytes (in their plasma cell form) that binds specifically to one type of antigen. Binding to antigens on a pathogen helps to eliminate it, for example by clumping pathogens together or marking them for destruction by phagocytes.

A molecule that the immune system recognizes as foreign and that triggers antibody production. Most antigens are glycoproteins or other proteins, and they are usually located on the outer surface of a pathogen. An antibody's binding site is specific to one antigen.

Glycoproteins and other molecules on the surface of erythrocytes that differ between people, for example between the ABO blood groups. If erythrocytes are transfused into a person whose blood group is different, the antigens they carry are foreign to the recipient and may stimulate antibody production, so donor and recipient blood must be matched.

A lymphocyte that does not produce antibodies but is needed to activate B-lymphocytes. Helper T-cells are antigen-specific: a helper T-cell becomes activated by a particular type of antigen and can then activate B-cells specific to that same antigen.

The process that a B-cell must undergo before it produces antibodies or becomes a memory cell. Activation requires two things: direct interaction of the B-cell with its specific antigen, and contact with a helper T-cell that has itself been activated by the same type of antigen.

A B-lymphocyte that has been activated and has differentiated to secrete large quantities of antibody. Plasma cells have extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus for the synthesis and secretion of antibody protein.

The large population of genetically identical plasma cells produced when an activated B-cell divides repeatedly by mitosis. Because there are only small numbers of B-cells specific to any one antigen, this multiplication is needed before enough antibody can be produced, and every cell in the clone makes the same type of antibody.

The ability to eliminate an infectious disease from the body. It is due to the long-term survival of lymphocytes (memory cells) that are capable of making the specific antibodies needed to fight the infection, not to the antibodies themselves persisting.

A long-lived lymphocyte formed when a B-cell (or T-cell) is activated. Memory cells do not secrete antibodies while the pathogen is absent; if the same antigen is encountered again they respond rapidly, dividing to form plasma cells so that antibody is produced sooner and in larger amounts than on first exposure.

Human immunodeficiency virus, a retrovirus that infects and eventually destroys certain lymphocytes. Infection with HIV is not the same as AIDS: a person can carry and transmit HIV for years before AIDS develops.

concepts.term: Transmission of HIV in body fluids
concepts.def: HIV is transmitted when body fluids containing the virus, such as blood, semen, vaginal secretions or breast milk, pass from one person into another. Mechanisms include unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing of hypodermic needles by drug users, transfusion of unscreened blood or blood products, and transmission from mother to child across the placenta, during birth or in breast milk. HIV is not transmitted by casual contact, saliva, sneezing or insect bites.

Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the condition that develops when HIV has killed so many helper T-lymphocytes that the adaptive immune system can no longer activate B-cells to produce antibodies. The person becomes unable to fight infections that a healthy immune system would control.

An infection by a pathogen that rarely causes disease in a person with a functioning immune system, but which takes the opportunity provided by a weakened immune system. The illnesses that characterize AIDS are opportunistic infections caused by other pathogens, not diseases caused directly by HIV.

A chemical that blocks a process occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells, so that it kills bacteria or stops them multiplying without harming the patient's cells. Examples of processes blocked are the synthesis of the peptidoglycan cell wall and protein synthesis on bacterial (70S) ribosomes.

Antibiotics do not control viral infections because viruses have no metabolism of their own: they lack cell walls, ribosomes and the enzymes that antibiotics target, and they reproduce using the metabolic processes of the host cell, which is a eukaryotic cell that antibiotics do not affect.

The ability of a strain of bacteria to survive and reproduce in the presence of an antibiotic that kills or inhibits other strains. Resistance arises by random mutation (or by acquiring a resistance gene from another bacterium) and then increases in frequency because the antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce: it is evolution by natural selection.

Strains of pathogenic bacteria that have accumulated resistance to several different antibiotics, each resistance requiring its own gene or mutation. Careful use of antibiotics, such as not prescribing them for viral infections and not using them unnecessarily in agriculture, reduces the selection pressure and slows the emergence of multiresistant strains.

concepts.term: Searching chemical libraries for new antibiotics (NOS)
concepts.def: A chemical library is a large collection of compounds that can be screened for a particular activity. Searching such libraries, in recent years with computer models trained to predict antibacterial activity, has identified candidate antibiotics with structures unlike existing ones. It illustrates that the development of a new technique can open up new avenues of research.

An infectious disease that can transfer from other species of animal to humans. A large proportion of human infectious diseases, and most newly emerging ones, are zoonoses, and their modes of infection are varied.

concepts.term: Tuberculosis, rabies and Japanese encephalitis as zoonoses
concepts.def: Three zoonoses with different modes of infection. Tuberculosis: the bacterium Mycobacterium bovis can pass from cattle to humans in unpasteurized milk (and by inhalation). Rabies: a virus in the saliva of an infected mammal, such as a dog or bat, enters through a bite. Japanese encephalitis: a virus carried from infected pigs and wading birds to humans by mosquitoes.

The disease caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which is thought to have transferred to humans from another species, most probably bats, shortly before it was identified in 2019. Having crossed into humans it then spread between people by respiratory droplets, causing a pandemic with profound consequences for human health, societies and economies.

A preparation that stimulates the development of immunity to a specific pathogen without causing the disease. A vaccine contains antigens of the pathogen (for example a killed or weakened pathogen, or purified antigen molecules), or nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) with a sequence coding for an antigen so that the person's own cells produce it. The antigen triggers an adaptive immune response that leaves memory cells.

The process of making a person immune to a disease, usually by vaccination. The vaccine's antigens activate specific B- and T-lymphocytes, which multiply and form memory cells, so a later infection by the real pathogen meets a rapid and effective response.

Protection of a whole population that arises when a sufficient percentage of its members are immune to a disease, so that transmission is greatly impeded and chains of infection are broken. Members of a population are interdependent: each immune person reduces the chance that a susceptible person, including one who cannot be vaccinated, is exposed. The percentage needed depends on how easily the disease spreads.

An outbreak in which the number of cases of an infectious disease in a population rises rapidly above the usual level. Epidemics can be prevented by keeping the immune fraction of the population above the level at which each infected person, on average, infects fewer than one other.

Scientific claims are accepted as pragmatic truths, reliable enough to act on because they have survived testing and evaluation, not as absolute certainties. Scientists publish research so that others can evaluate it; the media often report results while that evaluation is still going on. Vaccines are tested rigorously and the risk of side effects is minimal but not nil, so decisions weigh a small risk against a large benefit.

The change in a quantity expressed as a percentage of its original value: percentage change = (final value − initial value) ÷ initial value × 100. It is negative for a decrease. The denominator is the initial value, not the final value.

A comparison of two values where neither is the original or a reference value, such as case rates in two regions. In the convention used here, percentage difference = (difference between the values) ÷ (mean of the two values) × 100. Because the mean is used as the reference, the result is the same whichever value is listed first. When a question names a different reference value, use that value as the denominator instead.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the organisms that cause infectious diseases in humans is correct?
options: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists all include species that are human pathogens, but archaea are not known to be.
Archaea, like bacteria, include many species that are human pathogens, because both groups are prokaryotes.
Only bacteria and viruses cause infectious diseases in humans; fungi and protists do not cause any.
Any microorganism that lives on or inside the human body is, by definition, a pathogen and a cause of disease.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pathogens cause infectious disease, and observation beat germ theory to it
mcqs.explain: A disease-causing organism is a pathogen, and the term is typically reserved for viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists. Archaea, although they are prokaryotes, are not known to cause any diseases in humans.
rationales: A disease-causing organism is a pathogen, and the term is typically reserved for viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists. Archaea, although they are prokaryotes, are not known to cause any diseases in humans.
A student who treats 'prokaryote' as meaning 'germ' picks this. Being a prokaryote does not make an organism a pathogen; archaea are not known to cause any human disease.
A student whose examples of infectious disease are all bacterial or viral picks this. Fungi and protists also include human pathogens, such as the causes of athlete's foot and malaria.
A student who equates microorganisms with 'germs' picks this. A pathogen is defined by causing disease; most microorganisms on the skin and in the gut cause none.

mcqs.q: In 1854 John Snow recorded the addresses of people who died of cholera in Soho, London, and found that the deaths clustered around one public water pump. The pump handle was removed and the outbreak subsided. At that time the germ theory of disease had not been established. What does this episode illustrate about how science makes progress?
options: A disease can be controlled only once the microorganism that causes it has been identified in the laboratory.
Careful observation of a pattern in the data can lead to effective control of a disease before its cause is known.
Once Snow's conclusion had been published, it was certain and did not need to be evaluated by other scientists.
Science progressed here by proving that every microorganism in the pump water was a pathogen that had to be removed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Pathogens cause infectious disease, and observation beat germ theory to it
mcqs.explain: Snow acted on the pattern of deaths, not on knowledge of the pathogen, and the control measure worked. Careful observation during the Vienna childbed fever and London cholera epidemics led to breakthroughs in the control of infectious disease decades before the bacteria responsible were generally recognized.
rationales: A student who assumes explanation must precede action picks this. The pump handle was removed, and deaths fell, decades before a bacterium was generally accepted as the cause of cholera; the observed pattern alone justified the action.

Snow acted on the pattern of deaths, not on knowledge of the pathogen, and the control measure worked. Careful observation during the Vienna childbed fever and London cholera epidemics led to breakthroughs in the control of infectious disease decades before the bacteria responsible were generally recognized.

A student who thinks publication settles a claim picks this. Snow's conclusion was contested for years and gained acceptance only as other evidence accumulated; publication starts evaluation rather than ending it.

A student who treats all microorganisms as pathogens picks this. The episode showed only that something in the pump water caused cholera; most microorganisms in water are harmless, and the progress lay in acting on the observed pattern, not in identifying any microorganism.

mcqs.q: Sebaceous glands in the skin secrete sebum. Which statement explains how sebum contributes to the skin's role as a primary defence against pathogens?
options: It thickens the dead outer layer of the skin, so that the physical barrier becomes much harder for pathogens to penetrate.
It carries antibodies out onto the skin surface, where they bind to any pathogens before these can penetrate into the skin.
It makes the skin surface a chemical barrier: its fatty acids keep the pH low, inhibiting the growth of many pathogens.
It is secreted only once the skin is infected, so it is part of the immune response rather than a barrier.
mcqs.specStatementText: Skin and mucous membranes stop pathogens getting in
mcqs.explain: The skin acts as both a physical and a chemical barrier. The physical barrier is the tough outer layer of dead cells; the chemical barrier is the acidic surface maintained by the fatty acids in sebum, which inhibits the growth of many pathogens.
rationales: A student who sees the skin as a physical barrier only picks this. Sebum is an oily secretion; it does not add to the dead cell layer. Its contribution is chemical, through the low pH it maintains.
A student who assumes every defence involves the immune system picks this. Sebum contains no antibodies; the primary defences are barriers that act without lymphocytes or antibodies.

The skin acts as both a physical and a chemical barrier. The physical barrier is the tough outer layer of dead cells; the chemical barrier is the acidic surface maintained by the fatty acids in sebum, which inhibits the growth of many pathogens.
A student who thinks secretions appear only during infection picks this. Sebum is produced continuously, so the acidic surface is a standing barrier that is in place before any pathogen arrives.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events that seal a cut in the skin?
options: Platelets release clotting factors; a cascade produces thrombin; thrombin converts fibrin to fibrinogen; fibrinogen then traps erythrocytes.
Platelets stick to each other and to the edges of the cut, forming a solid plug that is itself the clot; no plasma proteins are involved at all.
Blood at the cut is exposed to the air, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin; the fibrin mesh then traps the platelets and erythrocytes to seal the cut.
Platelets release clotting factors; a cascade produces thrombin; thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin; fibrin traps erythrocytes.
mcqs.specStatementText: Clotting seals a cut
mcqs.explain: Clotting factors released from platelets start the cascade pathway, which results in rapid conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin by thrombin. The fibrin mesh traps erythrocytes, forming the clot that seals the cut.
rationales: A student who believes fibrin is the form that circulates picks this reversed sequence. Fibrinogen is the soluble circulating protein; thrombin converts it to insoluble fibrin, which forms the mesh.

A student who has learned only that 'platelets help clotting' picks this. Platelets start the process by releasing clotting factors, but the clot is a mesh of fibrin, made from the plasma protein fibrinogen, trapping erythrocytes.

A student who thinks air triggers clotting picks this. The trigger is the release of clotting factors from platelets at the damaged site; clots form inside the body, with no air present, by the same cascade.

Clotting factors released from platelets start the cascade pathway, which results in rapid conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin by thrombin. The fibrin mesh traps erythrocytes, forming the clot that seals the cut.

mcqs.q: Fibrinogen circulates in the plasma of healthy people all the time, yet clots form only where a blood vessel has been damaged. Which statement best explains this?
options: Thrombin, the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, is produced by a cascade that starts only when platelets release clotting factors at a site of damage.
Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin only when it is exposed to the air at an open wound, so a clot cannot form inside a vessel that is intact.
Fibrin is already present in the plasma, but its threads only become tangled into a mesh where the flow of blood is disturbed by damage.
The cascade has so many steps that it is too slow to finish unless the blood is held still against the wall of a damaged vessel.
mcqs.specStatementText: Clotting seals a cut
mcqs.explain: Fibrinogen is soluble and harmless while it circulates. Its conversion to insoluble fibrin requires thrombin, and thrombin is produced only at the end of the cascade pathway that the release of clotting factors from platelets initiates at the damaged site.
rationales: Fibrinogen is soluble and harmless while it circulates. Its conversion to insoluble fibrin requires thrombin, and thrombin is produced only at the end of the cascade pathway that the release of clotting factors from platelets initiates at the damaged site.

A student who thinks air causes clotting picks this. Clots can and do form inside intact vessels when the cascade is triggered inappropriately; the trigger is damage and the release of clotting factors, not contact with air.
A student who believes fibrin circulates ready-made picks this. The circulating protein is soluble fibrinogen; insoluble fibrin is produced only where thrombin has been generated by the cascade.

A student who reads 'cascade' as a delay picks this. The cascade amplifies the signal, which is why the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin is rapid; its confinement to the wound is due to where the clotting factors are released.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the innate immune system from the adaptive immune system?
options: Both systems build up a memory of the pathogens they meet, but the innate system does so faster because it does not need to be specific to each one.
The innate system responds to broad categories of pathogen and does not change during life; the adaptive system is specific and builds a memory of pathogens.
The innate system is the specific one, with each phagocyte recognizing just a single type of pathogen, while the lymphocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen.
The adaptive system responds faster than the innate system on first exposure to a pathogen, because a specific response is a more efficient response.
mcqs.specStatementText: Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
mcqs.explain: This is the distinction the IB draws. The innate response (including phagocytes) is the same on every exposure, whereas the adaptive response is specific to particular pathogens and becomes more effective because a memory of pathogens encountered is retained.
rationales: A student who applies 'building up immunity' to the whole immune system picks this. Only the adaptive system builds a memory; the innate system does not change during an organism's life.

This is the distinction the IB draws. The innate response (including phagocytes) is the same on every exposure, whereas the adaptive response is specific to particular pathogens and becomes more effective because a memory of pathogens encountered is retained.
A student who has attached specificity to the wrong cells picks this. Phagocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen; it is the lymphocytes of the adaptive system that are specific.

A student who assumes the more effective system must be the quicker one picks this. On first exposure the adaptive response takes days, because the few specific lymphocytes must be activated and multiply; the innate response is immediate.

mcqs.q: A person is infected by the same strain of a virus twice, two years apart. The second time, the number of virus particles in the blood peaks at a much lower level and falls to zero in half the time. Which explanation is correct?
options: Phagocytes of the innate immune system had learned to recognize this virus during the first infection, so they engulfed it faster the second time.
Antibodies made during the first infection had stayed in the blood at their peak concentration for two years and destroyed the virus at once.
The adaptive immune system had retained a memory of the virus, so its specific response was faster and more effective the second time.
The phagocytes specific to this virus had multiplied during the first infection and were still present in large numbers.
mcqs.specStatementText: Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
mcqs.explain: The adaptive system responds in a specific way to particular pathogens and builds up a memory of pathogens encountered, so the immune response becomes more effective. Memory cells from the first infection allowed antibody to be produced sooner and in greater quantity.
rationales: A student who credits the innate system with improvement picks this. The innate system does not change during an organism's life; phagocytes respond in the same way to a pathogen however often it is met.

A student who equates immunity with persisting antibodies picks this. Antibodies are broken down over months, and the data show the virus still multiplied to a peak; what persists is memory cells, which produce a fresh and faster supply of antibody on re-exposure.

The adaptive system responds in a specific way to particular pathogens and builds up a memory of pathogens encountered, so the immune response becomes more effective. Memory cells from the first infection allowed antibody to be produced sooner and in greater quantity.

A student who thinks phagocytes are specific picks this. Phagocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen and are not specific to one virus; the specific, multiplying, memory-forming cells are lymphocytes.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium?
options: It secretes enzymes from its lysosomes onto the bacterium, digesting it outside the cell, and then absorbs the soluble products.
It lets the bacterium pass straight through its plasma membrane into the cytoplasm, where cytoplasmic enzymes break it down.
It binds to the bacterium using a receptor specific to that strain and holds it until lymphocytes arrive to destroy it.
It engulfs the bacterium by endocytosis and then digests it inside the cell, using the enzymes from its lysosomes.
mcqs.specStatementText: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens
mcqs.explain: Phagocytes recognize pathogens, engulf them by endocytosis so that the pathogen is enclosed in a vesicle, and digest them using enzymes from lysosomes that fuse with the vesicle.
rationales: A student who pictures the external digestion of fungi picks this. Phagocytes engulf the pathogen first; the lysosomal enzymes act inside a vesicle within the cell, not on the outside.

A student who thinks 'engulfing' means passing through the membrane picks this. Endocytosis encloses the bacterium in a membrane-bound vesicle; it never enters the cytoplasm freely, and the enzymes come from lysosomes.
A student who thinks phagocytes are specific and only lymphocytes kill picks this. Phagocytes recognize broad categories of pathogen and destroy them themselves, by engulfing and digesting them.
Phagocytes recognize pathogens, engulf them by endocytosis so that the pathogen is enclosed in a vesicle, and digest them using enzymes from lysosomes that fuse with the vesicle.

mcqs.q: A splinter carrying bacteria lodges in the connective tissue of a finger, some distance from the nearest capillary. Within hours the bacteria are being destroyed by phagocytes. Which statement describes how this happens?
options: Phagocytes leave the capillary by amoeboid movement, crawl through the tissue to the bacteria, then engulf them by endocytosis and digest them.
Phagocytes remain inside the capillary; tissue fluid carries the bacteria into the blood, where the phagocytes engulf and digest them.
Phagocytes in the capillary secrete lysosomal enzymes into the tissue fluid, which diffuse to the splinter and digest the bacteria there.
Only the few phagocytes that carry a receptor specific to this strain of bacterium respond to it; the rest ignore the infection.
mcqs.specStatementText: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens
mcqs.explain: Infection control by phagocytes includes amoeboid movement from blood to sites of infection, where the phagocytes recognize pathogens, engulf them by endocytosis and digest them using enzymes from lysosomes.
rationales: Infection control by phagocytes includes amoeboid movement from blood to sites of infection, where the phagocytes recognize pathogens, engulf them by endocytosis and digest them using enzymes from lysosomes.

A student who thinks 'white blood cells' stay in the blood picks this. Phagocytes move out of capillaries by amoeboid movement and go to the site of infection; the bacteria are destroyed in the tissue.
A student who imagines external digestion picks this. Phagocytes do not release their enzymes into the tissue; they engulf the bacteria and digest them inside a vesicle using enzymes from lysosomes.

A student who has transferred lymphocyte specificity to phagocytes picks this. Phagocytes belong to the innate system and respond to broad categories of pathogen, so any phagocyte reaching the splinter can engulf the bacteria.

mcqs.q: Which statement about B-lymphocytes and antibodies is correct?
options: Each B-lymphocyte examines the antigen it meets and then adjusts the shape of the antibody it makes so that it fits the antigen.
A person has a very large number of different B-lymphocytes, and each of them makes a single specific type of antibody.
Helper T-cells and B-lymphocytes both secrete antibodies, which is why they are said to cooperate in producing them.
B-lymphocytes are found only in the blood; lymph nodes contain trapped pathogens but no lymphocytes at all.
mcqs.specStatementText: Lymphocytes cooperate to make antibodies
mcqs.explain: An individual has a very large number of B-lymphocytes that each make a specific type of antibody. The diversity of B-cells, not any tailoring by an individual cell, is what allows a specific response to almost any antigen.
rationales: A student who reads 'adaptive' as tailoring picks this. The antibody a B-cell makes is fixed before it meets any antigen; the antigen selects the B-cells that already fit it.

An individual has a very large number of B-lymphocytes that each make a specific type of antibody. The diversity of B-cells, not any tailoring by an individual cell, is what allows a specific response to almost any antigen.
A student who reads 'cooperate' as both making antibody picks this. Only B-lymphocytes produce antibodies; helper T-cells cooperate by activating them.
A student who knows lymphocytes only as white blood cells picks this. Lymphocytes both circulate in the blood and are contained in lymph nodes, which is where many antigens meet them.

mcqs.q: Which statement about antigens is correct?
options: Antigens are proteins made by lymphocytes that bind to pathogens and mark them for destruction by the phagocytes.
Antigens are toxins released by a pathogen into the blood, and it is these toxins that the antibodies must neutralize.
Most antigens are glycoproteins or other proteins, usually located on the outer surface of a pathogen.
Antigens are found only on pathogens; molecules on the surface of human cells do not act as antigens.
mcqs.specStatementText: Antigens are the foreign molecules that trigger the response
mcqs.explain: Antigens are recognition molecules that trigger antibody production. Most are glycoproteins or other proteins, and they are usually located on the outer surfaces of pathogens, where they can be recognized by the immune system.
rationales: A student who has swapped the two 'anti-' words picks this. The molecules made by lymphocytes that bind to pathogens are antibodies; antigens are the molecules on the pathogen that they bind to.
A student who merges antigens with toxins picks this. An antigen is a molecule on the surface of the pathogen that is recognized as foreign; a pathogen has antigens whether or not it produces toxins.

Antigens are recognition molecules that trigger antibody production. Most are glycoproteins or other proteins, and they are usually located on the outer surfaces of pathogens, where they can be recognized by the immune system.
A student who defines antigens by their source picks this. Antigens on the surface of human erythrocytes stimulate antibody production if transfused into a person with a different blood group.

mcqs.q: In an experiment, B-lymphocytes specific to an antigen were cultured with that antigen and no other cells. No antibody was produced. When helper T-lymphocytes were added to the culture, antibody production began. What does this show?
options: A B-lymphocyte is activated to produce antibodies only when it both binds its specific antigen and makes contact with a helper T-lymphocyte.
Binding of the antigen alone should have activated the B-lymphocytes, so the first culture must have been set up incorrectly.
The antibody in the second culture was secreted by the helper T-lymphocytes, which make antibody when they meet an antigen.
The helper T-lymphocytes showed the B-lymphocytes the shape of the antigen so that they could then design an antibody to fit it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Helper T-cells switch B-cells on
mcqs.explain: B-cells produce antibodies only when they have been activated, and activation requires both direct interaction with the specific antigen and contact with a helper T-cell. Antigen alone was not sufficient; adding the helper T-cells supplied the missing requirement.
rationales: B-cells produce antibodies only when they have been activated, and activation requires both direct interaction with the specific antigen and contact with a helper T-cell. Antigen alone was not sufficient; adding the helper T-cells supplied the missing requirement.
A student who holds the one-step story picks this. The first culture behaved as expected: antigen binding is necessary but not sufficient, and without helper T-cell contact no activation occurs.
A student who thinks T-cells make antibodies picks this. Helper T-cells secrete no antibody; their role is to activate the B-cells, which then produce it.
A student who imagines antibodies being designed picks this. The B-cells in the culture already made an antibody that fitted the antigen; what they lacked was activation by a helper T-cell.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the transmission of HIV is correct?
options: HIV is transmitted in body fluids such as blood, semen, vaginal secretions and breast milk, for example through unprotected sex, shared needles or from mother to child.
HIV is transmitted through the air by coughing, and by casual contact such as shaking hands, sharing cutlery or using the same toilet as an infected person.
HIV is transmitted by blood-feeding insects such as mosquitoes, in the same way as the virus that causes Japanese encephalitis is transmitted.
HIV can only be transmitted by a person who has already developed AIDS, because before that stage the virus is not present in body fluids.
mcqs.specStatementText: HIV passes only in certain body fluids
mcqs.explain: HIV is transmitted in body fluids. The mechanisms include unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing of hypodermic needles, transfusion of unscreened blood or blood products, and transmission from mother to child across the placenta, during birth or in breast milk.
rationales: HIV is transmitted in body fluids. The mechanisms include unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing of hypodermic needles, transfusion of unscreened blood or blood products, and transmission from mother to child across the placenta, during birth or in breast milk.

A student who generalizes from colds and contact infections picks this. HIV is not present in sufficient quantity in saliva or on skin, does not survive outside the body and is not transmitted by these routes.
A student who knows HIV is in blood and that mosquitoes carry some viruses picks this. HIV does not replicate in mosquitoes and is not transmitted by insect bites.
A student who treats HIV and AIDS as the same thing picks this. A person with HIV is infectious from soon after infection, often for years before AIDS develops.

mcqs.q: A person with untreated HIV infection eventually becomes unable to produce antibodies against new pathogens, even though tests show that B-lymphocytes are still present in their blood in substantial numbers. Which statement explains this?
options: HIV infects and kills the B-lymphocytes that make the antibodies, so the cells that are needed for antibody production are no longer present in the blood.
HIV infects and kills helper T-lymphocytes, and without contact with an activated helper T-cell a B-lymphocyte cannot be activated to make antibodies.
Antibodies are secreted by the helper T-lymphocytes, so when HIV destroys these cells the production of all antibodies stops.
HIV infects and destroys all types of white blood cell, so every part of the immune system, including antibody production, fails at once.
mcqs.specStatementText: HIV kills helper T-cells, and AIDS follows
mcqs.explain: Only certain types of lymphocyte are infected and killed by HIV, principally helper T-cells. Because B-cell activation requires contact with an activated helper T-cell, the reduction in helper T-cells limits the ability to produce antibodies even though the B-cells themselves survive.
rationales: A student who reasons backwards from the lost antibodies to the cell that makes them picks this. The stem states that B-cells are still present in substantial numbers; it is the helper T-cells that HIV destroys.

Only certain types of lymphocyte are infected and killed by HIV, principally helper T-cells. Because B-cell activation requires contact with an activated helper T-cell, the reduction in helper T-cells limits the ability to produce antibodies even though the B-cells themselves survive.
A student who thinks T-cells make antibodies picks this. Helper T-cells produce no antibody; they activate the B-cells, and it is the loss of that activation that stops antibody production.
A student who pictures the whole immune system being wiped out picks this. HIV infects only certain lymphocytes; the B-cells in the stem are present but cannot be activated.

mcqs.q: Two people infected with HIV were compared. Person X had 900 helper T-lymphocytes per mm³ of blood and no other infections. Person Y had 150 helper T-lymphocytes per mm³ and had developed pneumonia caused by a fungus that rarely causes disease in healthy people. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The pneumonia in person Y is caused directly by HIV, which has spread from the blood into the lungs as the infection has progressed.
Person Y's B-lymphocytes have all been destroyed by HIV, which is why antibodies against the fungus have not been produced.
Person Y's loss of helper T-lymphocytes has limited antibody production and defence against infection, so an opportunistic infection has taken hold.
Person X cannot really be infected with HIV, because HIV and AIDS are the same condition and person X shows no symptoms of any disease.
mcqs.specStatementText: HIV kills helper T-cells, and AIDS follows
mcqs.explain: HIV kills helper T-cells, and a reduction in these lymphocytes limits the ability to produce antibodies and fight opportunistic infections. Person Y's low count and a fungal pneumonia that healthy people resist together indicate that AIDS has developed.
rationales: A student who treats AIDS as a single disease caused by HIV picks this. The stem states that the pneumonia is caused by a fungus; it is an opportunistic infection that the weakened immune system cannot eliminate.
A student who assumes the antibody-producing cell must be the target picks this. The data are about helper T-cells, which HIV kills; B-cells survive but cannot be activated without them.

HIV kills helper T-cells, and a reduction in these lymphocytes limits the ability to produce antibodies and fight opportunistic infections. Person Y's low count and a fungal pneumonia that healthy people resist together indicate that AIDS has developed.

A student who equates HIV with AIDS picks this. A person can carry HIV for years with a helper T-cell count high enough to prevent opportunistic infections; AIDS develops only when the count has fallen far.

mcqs.q: Why do antibiotics fail to control infections caused by viruses?
options: Viruses are far smaller than bacteria, so antibiotic molecules are too large to bind to them or to enter them effectively.
Antibiotics would destroy the human cells inside which viruses replicate, so they cannot safely be used against a viral infection.
They do not fail: antibiotics kill viruses as well as bacteria, only more slowly, so a longer course is needed for a viral infection.
Viruses have no metabolic processes of their own; they use those of the host cell, which antibiotics do not block.
mcqs.specStatementText: Antibiotics hit bacterial processes, which viruses do not have
mcqs.explain: Antibiotics are chemicals that block processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells. A virus has no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of its own: it reproduces using the eukaryotic host cell's processes, which antibiotics leave untouched.
rationales: A student who reaches for size as the explanation picks this. The reason is biochemical: an antibiotic blocks a bacterial process, and a virus has no equivalent process to block, whatever its size.

A student who thinks antibiotics damage human cells picks this. Antibiotics are selective for bacterial processes and do not harm eukaryotic cells; they fail against viruses because there is nothing for them to act on.
A student who sees antibiotics as general anti-infection drugs picks this. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses at any dose or duration, because viruses lack the processes that antibiotics block.

Antibiotics are chemicals that block processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells. A virus has no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of its own: it reproduces using the eukaryotic host cell's processes, which antibiotics leave untouched.

mcqs.q: Penicillin blocks the enzymes that build cross-links in the peptidoglycan cell wall of bacteria. A patient takes penicillin for a bacterial infection. Why does the drug kill the bacteria without harming the patient's own cells?
options: Human cells have no cell wall and do not synthesize peptidoglycan, so the process that penicillin blocks does not occur in the patient's cells at all.
Penicillin does damage the patient's cells in the same way, but the patient has so many more cells that the loss is not noticeable.
Penicillin cannot reach the inside of human cells, so it only acts on bacteria, which live outside cells in the blood and tissues.
The patient's cells have evolved resistance to penicillin, because humans have now been exposed to the drug for several generations.
mcqs.specStatementText: Antibiotics hit bacterial processes, which viruses do not have
mcqs.explain: Antibiotics are chemicals that block processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells. Peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis is one such process: bacteria depend on it, eukaryotic cells do not carry it out, so penicillin is selective.
rationales: Antibiotics are chemicals that block processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells. Peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis is one such process: bacteria depend on it, eukaryotic cells do not carry it out, so penicillin is selective.

A student who assumes any cell-killing drug is indiscriminate picks this. Penicillin's target does not exist in human cells, so it does not damage them; selectivity, not cell numbers, is the explanation.

A student who explains antibiotic selectivity by where the drug can reach picks this. Selectivity is biochemical: human cells lack peptidoglycan and the enzymes that build it, so there is no target for penicillin whether or not the drug enters them.

A student who thinks resistance is a property of people picks this. Resistance evolves in bacterial populations under selection; human cells were never affected by penicillin, so there was nothing to become resistant to.

mcqs.q: A hospital ward uses one particular antibiotic heavily. Over several years, an increasing proportion of the bacteria isolated from patients on the ward are found to be resistant to it. Which statement correctly explains this change?
options: Repeated exposure to the antibiotic caused individual bacteria to develop resistance during their own lifetimes, and they passed on this acquired trait to their offspring.
Random mutations had given a few bacteria resistance; the antibiotic killed the susceptible ones, so resistant bacteria survived, reproduced and became more common.
The patients on the ward gradually became resistant to the antibiotic, so it stopped working against the bacteria that were infecting them.
The bacteria became resistant to every antibiotic at the same time, because a single mutation makes a bacterium generally tougher against all drugs.
mcqs.specStatementText: Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
mcqs.explain: Resistance evolves by natural selection. Variation from random mutation (or acquired genes) exists before exposure; heavy use of the antibiotic removes the susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce, so the resistant proportion rises over time.
rationales: A student who thinks resistance is a response to exposure picks this. The antibiotic does not cause resistance in an individual bacterium; it selects for bacteria that already carry a resistance mutation.

Resistance evolves by natural selection. Variation from random mutation (or acquired genes) exists before exposure; heavy use of the antibiotic removes the susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce, so the resistant proportion rises over time.
A student who locates resistance in the patient picks this. Resistance is a heritable property of the bacterial strain, which is why it is detected in bacteria isolated from patients.

A student who pictures a 'superbug' as generally hardier picks this. Resistance is specific to the process each antibiotic blocks; resistance to several drugs requires several separate genes or mutations.

mcqs.q: Researchers screened a chemical library of thousands of compounds using a computer model trained to predict antibacterial activity. They identified a compound, structurally unlike any existing antibiotic, that killed several multiresistant strains of bacteria in the laboratory. Which statement is the best evaluation of this work?
options: Because the compound kills multiresistant strains, bacteria will not be able to evolve resistance to it, since they have not previously encountered it.
Because the results have been published, the compound can be regarded as a proven antibiotic that is ready to be given to patients.
A new technique has opened a new avenue of research; the compound still needs testing, and careful use of antibiotics is still necessary.
Because new antibiotics can now be found by searching chemical libraries, there is no longer any need to limit the use of the existing antibiotics.
mcqs.specStatementText: Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
mcqs.explain: The NOS point is that the development of new techniques, such as searching chemical libraries, can lead to new avenues of research and is yielding new antibiotics. A laboratory hit is a candidate, not a medicine, and any antibiotic will select for resistance if used carelessly.
rationales: A student who thinks resistance is a reaction to a drug's history picks this. Resistance arises by random mutation and selection; a new antibiotic will select for resistant variants just as older ones did.

A student who thinks publication settles a claim picks this. Publication allows other scientists to evaluate the work; a laboratory result must survive further testing, including trials in humans, before use.

The NOS point is that the development of new techniques, such as searching chemical libraries, can lead to new avenues of research and is yielding new antibiotics. A laboratory hit is a candidate, not a medicine, and any antibiotic will select for resistance if used carelessly.
A student who sees discovery as the whole solution picks this. Every antibiotic in use selects for resistance, so careful use is still necessary to slow the emergence of multiresistant bacteria.

mcqs.q: A farm worker develops tuberculosis after drinking unpasteurized milk from a cow infected with the bacterium Mycobacterium bovis. Which statement about this infection is correct?
options: It is not a zoonosis, because zoonoses are transmitted only by animal bites or by insect vectors, not in food.
It is not a zoonosis, because tuberculosis is a human disease that only occasionally infects cattle and other animals.
It cannot be a zoonosis, because only viruses can cross from one species to another; bacteria stay in one host.
It is a zoonosis, because the pathogen has transferred from another species of animal to a human.
mcqs.specStatementText: Many human diseases come from other animals
mcqs.explain: A zoonosis is an infectious disease that can transfer from other species to humans. Tuberculosis is one of the examples the IB names: Mycobacterium bovis infects cattle and can be transmitted to people in unpasteurized milk.
rationales: A student who generalizes from rabies and mosquito-borne diseases picks this. The modes of infection of zoonoses are varied; transfer in milk from an infected cow qualifies just as a bite does.
A student who assumes familiar diseases are purely human picks this. Mycobacterium bovis is a pathogen of cattle that transfers to humans, which is exactly what makes bovine tuberculosis a zoonosis.
A student whose zoonosis examples are all viral picks this. Bacteria such as Mycobacterium bovis transfer between species too; zoonoses include bacterial as well as viral pathogens.

A zoonosis is an infectious disease that can transfer from other species to humans. Tuberculosis is one of the examples the IB names: Mycobacterium bovis infects cattle and can be transmitted to people in unpasteurized milk.

mcqs.q: Which statement about COVID-19 is correct?
options: It is a zoonosis: SARS-CoV-2 is thought to have transferred to humans from another species recently, and it then spread widely between people.
It is a zoonosis, which means that every case of COVID-19 was caught directly from an infected animal rather than from another person.
It is not a zoonosis, because SARS-CoV-2 arose within the human population, and diseases only very rarely transfer from animals to humans.
It is not a zoonosis, because it spreads from person to person by respiratory droplets rather than by animal bites or insect vectors.
mcqs.specStatementText: Many human diseases come from other animals
mcqs.explain: COVID-19 is an infectious disease that has recently transferred from another species. Once in humans, SARS-CoV-2 spread from person to person by respiratory droplets, causing a pandemic with profound consequences for human health, societies and economies.
rationales: COVID-19 is an infectious disease that has recently transferred from another species. Once in humans, SARS-CoV-2 spread from person to person by respiratory droplets, causing a pandemic with profound consequences for human health, societies and economies.

A student who thinks a zoonosis must come from an animal each time picks this. Zoonosis refers to the original transfer from another species; COVID-19 then spread between humans, which is what made it a pandemic.
A student who thinks zoonoses are rare picks this. Most newly emerging human infections are zoonoses, and SARS-CoV-2 is thought to have come from another species, most probably bats.
A student who defines zoonoses by a bite or vector route picks this. A zoonosis is defined by transfer from another species, not by the route; the modes of infection are varied.

mcqs.q: An mRNA vaccine against COVID-19 contains RNA with the sequence coding for the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, packaged in lipid nanoparticles. Which statement correctly explains how it stimulates immunity?
options: The RNA is translated into antibodies against the spike protein, which then circulate in the blood ready to bind to the virus.
Cells translate the RNA into spike protein, an antigen that stimulates the adaptive immune system to form memory cells without causing disease.
The RNA produces a weakened form of the whole virus inside the person's cells, giving a mild case of COVID-19 that generates immunity.
The RNA is copied into the DNA of the person's chromosomes, so that their cells will permanently carry and express the gene for the viral antigen.
mcqs.specStatementText: Vaccines deliver antigens, not the disease
mcqs.explain: Vaccines contain antigens, or nucleic acids with sequences that code for antigens, and stimulate the development of immunity to a specific pathogen without causing the disease. The person's cells make the spike protein, and the adaptive response to it leaves memory cells.
rationales: A student who thinks vaccines supply antibodies picks this. The RNA codes for the antigen, not for antibodies; the person's own B-lymphocytes make the antibodies in response to it.

Vaccines contain antigens, or nucleic acids with sequences that code for antigens, and stimulate the development of immunity to a specific pathogen without causing the disease. The person's cells make the spike protein, and the adaptive response to it leaves memory cells.
A student who thinks a vaccine is a mild dose of the disease picks this. The RNA codes for one protein only; no virus is assembled and the disease does not occur.
A student who blurs RNA and DNA picks this. The mRNA is translated in the cytoplasm and then degraded; it does not enter the nucleus or alter the person's genome, and antigen production is temporary.

mcqs.q: For measles, transmission in a population is greatly impeded once about 95% of people are immune. A community's vaccination coverage falls from 96% to 85%. Which statement correctly describes a consequence?
options: The unvaccinated people remain immune too, because herd immunity continues to protect the whole population permanently once it has been reached.
Only the people who chose not to be vaccinated are affected, because each person's vaccination status affects only their own risk of infection.
People who are not immune, including those who cannot be vaccinated, are at greater risk because chains of transmission are no longer broken.
There is no consequence, because measles was eliminated from the community while coverage was above 95% and so cannot return.
mcqs.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
mcqs.explain: Members of a population are interdependent in building herd immunity. If a sufficient percentage is immune, transmission is greatly impeded; below that level the virus can pass from case to case, and everyone who is susceptible, whatever the reason, is more likely to be exposed.
rationales: A student who takes 'immunity' literally picks this. Unvaccinated people were never immune; they were shielded by the high immune fraction, and that shield weakens as coverage falls.
A student who sees vaccination as a purely personal choice picks this. Falling coverage also endangers infants and people who cannot be vaccinated, who depended on others to block transmission.

Members of a population are interdependent in building herd immunity. If a sufficient percentage is immune, transmission is greatly impeded; below that level the virus can pass from case to case, and everyone who is susceptible, whatever the reason, is more likely to be exposed.

A student who thinks herd immunity removes a pathogen for good picks this. Herd immunity only impedes transmission while the immune percentage stays high; measles can be reintroduced and spread once coverage falls.

mcqs.q: A news article reports a newly published study claiming that a vaccine causes a rare side effect, before other scientists have evaluated the study. Which response shows the best understanding of how science works?
options: Accept the claim as established, because a study that has been published in a scientific journal has been proven to be correct.
Conclude that the vaccine is unsafe, because a vaccine that is genuinely safe would carry no risk of side effects of any kind.
Dismiss the claim without reading it, because vaccines are tested so rigorously that a side effect of any kind is impossible.
Treat the claim as provisional until other scientists have evaluated the study; vaccine risks are minimal but not nil.
mcqs.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
mcqs.explain: Scientists publish so that others can evaluate their work, and the media often report while evaluation is still happening. Vaccines are tested rigorously and side effects are minimal but not nil, so a new claim deserves evaluation rather than immediate acceptance or dismissal.
rationales: A student who thinks publication is proof picks this. Publication begins evaluation by other scientists; a published claim is provisional until it has survived that scrutiny.
A student who treats safety as an absolute picks this. Risks of side effects are minimal but not nil; a rare side effect does not make a vaccine unsafe if the benefit greatly outweighs it.

A student who confuses well-supported with certain picks this. Rigorous testing makes side effects very unlikely, not impossible; science offers pragmatic truths, and new evidence should be evaluated.

Scientists publish so that others can evaluate their work, and the media often report while evaluation is still happening. Vaccines are tested rigorously and side effects are minimal but not nil, so a new claim deserves evaluation rather than immediate acceptance or dismissal.

mcqs.q: In a country, the number of new COVID-19 cases recorded per day fell from 2000 in one week to 1600 in the following week. What is the percentage change in the daily number of cases?
options: Fell by 20%
Fell by 25%
Fell by 22%
Fell by 80%
mcqs.specStatementText: Percentage change and percentage difference
mcqs.explain: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (1600 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = −400 ÷ 2000 × 100 = −20%, a fall of 20%.
rationales: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (1600 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = −400 ÷ 2000 × 100 = −20%, a fall of 20%.
A student who divides the change by the final value picks this: 400 ÷ 1600 × 100 = 25%. Percentage change is measured relative to the initial value, 2000.

A student who applies the percentage difference formula picks this: 400 ÷ 1800 × 100 = 22%. Percentage difference uses the mean of the two values and is for comparing two groups; a change over time uses the initial value as the reference.
A student who divides the new value by the old value picks this: 1600 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 80% is the new figure as a percentage of the old one. The change is 80% − 100% = −20%.

mcqs.q: In one week, region P recorded 640 COVID-19 hospital admissions per million people and region Q recorded 960 per million. Taking the mean of the two rates as the reference value, what is the percentage difference between the two regions' admission rates, to the nearest whole number?
mcqs.specStatementText: Percentage change and percentage difference
mcqs.explain: Percentage difference = difference ÷ mean × 100. The difference is 960 − 640 = 320 and the mean is (640 + 960) ÷ 2 = 800, so 320 ÷ 800 × 100 = 40%.
rationales: A student who divides the difference by one of the values, as in a percentage change, picks this: 320 ÷ 640 × 100 = 50%. Neither region is the 'original', and the stem sets the mean, 800, as the reference.
Percentage difference = difference ÷ mean × 100. The difference is 960 − 640 = 320 and the mean is (640 + 960) ÷ 2 = 800, so 320 ÷ 800 × 100 = 40%.
A student who divides by the larger value picks this: 320 ÷ 960 × 100 = 33%. Percentage difference is symmetrical because it uses the mean of the two values, not either value alone.
A student who divides by the sum of the two values picks this: 320 ÷ 1600 × 100 = 20%. The denominator is the mean, (640 + 960) ÷ 2 = 800, so the answer is twice this.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C3.2 Defence against disease

specStatements.text: Pathogens cause infectious disease, and observation beat germ theory to it
Skin and mucous membranes stop pathogens getting in
Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
Antigens are the foreign molecules that trigger the response
Activated B-cells multiply into a clone of plasma cells
Memory cells are why immunity lasts
HIV passes only in certain body fluids
HIV kills helper T-cells, and AIDS follows
Antibiotics hit bacterial processes, which viruses do not have
Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
Many human diseases come from other animals
Vaccines deliver antigens, not the disease
Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No object asks for the layers or structures of skin by position or name beyond the outer dead layer and sebaceous glands. The skin is treated only as a physical barrier and, through sebum, as a chemical barrier; the epidermis, dermis, hair follicles and sweat glands are neither named nor tested.

Clotting is described only as: platelets release clotting factors, a cascade follows, thrombin rapidly converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and fibrin traps erythrocytes to form a clot. Prothrombin, calcium ions, vitamin K, numbered clotting factors, the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways and clot retraction are not named or tested.

Phagocytes are the only innate cells or molecules named. Complement, natural killer cells, inflammation, cytokines, interferon, fever and lysozyme are not mentioned anywhere in the bank, and the difference between the two systems is tested only in terms of breadth of response, change over life and memory.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
